Let \(\theta=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)^T\), \(Z=(1,X_1,X_2)^T\), and  
\[
\pi_\theta(x)=\frac{\exp(\theta^T z)}{1+\exp(\theta^T z)}.
\]

A note on the numerical parts: the prompt here does not include the actual R data-generation code, in particular the values of \(n_1,n\), test-set size, and object names. Therefore the exact numerical coefficients/test scores cannot be uniquely recovered from the text alone. Below I give the exact R code that reports the requested numbers when run on the supplied `set.seed(1)` data.

---

## 1) Why the logistic model is misspecified

The true posterior log-odds are

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
\]

because \(P(Y=1)=P(Y=0)=1/2\), where

\[
f_0=N\left((-6,-6),\operatorname{diag}(5^2,15^2)\right),
\qquad
f_1=N\left((6,6),\operatorname{diag}(5^2,10^2)\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\log\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
=
-\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_1|}{|\Sigma_0|}
-\frac12\left\{(x-\mu_1)^T\Sigma_1^{-1}(x-\mu_1)
-(x-\mu_0)^T\Sigma_0^{-1}(x-\mu_0)\right\}.
\]

Here

\[
\mu_0=(-6,-6)^T,\quad \mu_1=(6,6)^T,
\]
\[
\Sigma_0=\operatorname{diag}(25,225),\quad
\Sigma_1=\operatorname{diag}(25,100).
\]

A direct expansion gives

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log(3/2)-0.1+\frac{12}{25}x_1+\frac{13}{150}x_2-\frac{1}{360}x_2^2.
\]

Therefore the true logit is quadratic in \(x_2\), not linear in \(x=(x_1,x_2)\). The assumed logistic model

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid x)}{P(Y=0\mid x)}
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2
\]

cannot represent the true conditional probability. Hence the logistic model is misspecified. Equivalently, unequal class covariances produce a quadratic discriminant boundary rather than a linear one.

---

## 2) Labeled-data MLE and test performance

The labeled logistic MLE maximizes

\[
\ell_\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
\left\{
Y_i\theta^T Z_i-\log\left(1+e^{\theta^T Z_i}\right)
\right\}.
\]

The test average log-likelihood on a test set \((X_j^{\mathrm{te}},Y_j^{\mathrm{te}})_{j=1}^m\) is

\[
\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m
\left[
Y_j^{\mathrm{te}}\eta_j-\log\{1+e^{\eta_j}\}
\right],
\qquad
\eta_j=\hat\theta^T Z_j^{\mathrm{te}}.
\]

The classification accuracy is

\[
\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m
1\left\{1(\eta_j\ge 0)=Y_j^{\mathrm{te}}\right\}.
\]

Assuming the supplied objects are:

- `xs`: \(n\times 2\) training covariate matrix,
- `ys`: length \(n\) vector of training labels, although only `ys[1:n1]` is used as labeled,
- `xstest`, `ystest`: test data,

the R code is:

```r
log1pexp <- function(a) {
  out <- numeric(length(a))
  idx <- a > 0
  out[idx] <- a[idx] + log1p(exp(-a[idx]))
  out[!idx] <- log1p(exp(a[!idx]))
  out
}

perf <- function(theta, Xtest, ytest) {
  Ztest <- cbind(1, as.matrix(Xtest))
  eta <- drop(Ztest %*% theta)
  avg.ll <- mean(ytest * eta - log1pexp(eta))
  acc <- mean((eta >= 0) == ytest)
  c(avg.test.loglik = avg.ll, test.accuracy = acc)
}

Xl <- xs[1:n1, ]
yl <- ys[1:n1]

dat.labeled <- data.frame(
  y = yl,
  x1 = Xl[, 1],
  x2 = Xl[, 2]
)

fit.hat <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial(), data = dat.labeled)

theta.hat <- unname(coef(fit.hat))
names(theta.hat) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

theta.hat
perf(theta.hat, xstest, ystest)
```

Running this on the supplied `set.seed(1)` data gives the requested \((\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta)\), average test log-likelihood, and accuracy.

---

## 3) A loss minimized by \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

The estimating equation is

\[
0=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i\le n_1}Y_i Z_i
-
\frac1n\sum_{i\le n}\pi_\theta(X_i) Z_i.
\]

Define

\[
L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\log\left(1+e^{\theta^T Z_i}\right)
-
\theta^T
\left[
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i Z_i
\right].
\]

Then

\[
\nabla_\theta L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi_\theta(X_i) Z_i
-
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i Z_i.
\]

Thus \(\nabla_\theta L_n(\tilde\theta)=0\) is exactly the given estimating equation.

Moreover,

\[
\nabla_\theta^2 L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\pi_\theta(X_i)\{1-\pi_\theta(X_i)\}Z_iZ_i^T,
\]

which is positive semidefinite. Under the usual full-rank design condition, it is positive definite, so \(L_n\) is convex and any solution of the estimating equation is the global minimizer.

---

## 4) Newton-Raphson function for \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

Newton-Raphson uses

\[
\theta^{(k+1)}
=
\theta^{(k)}
-
\left\{\nabla^2 L_n(\theta^{(k)})\right\}^{-1}
\nabla L_n(\theta^{(k)}).
\]

Here is an R implementation.

```r
ssl_logit_newton <- function(Xl, yl, Xu,
                             start = NULL,
                             tol = 1e-10,
                             maxit = 100,
                             trace = FALSE) {
  Xl <- as.matrix(Xl)
  Xu <- as.matrix(Xu)
  yl <- as.numeric(yl)

  X <- rbind(Xl, Xu)

  Z <- cbind(1, X)
  Zl <- cbind(1, Xl)

  n <- nrow(Z)
  n1 <- nrow(Zl)
  p <- ncol(Z)

  b <- drop(crossprod(Zl, yl)) / n1

  log1pexp <- function(a) {
    out <- numeric(length(a))
    idx <- a > 0
    out[idx] <- a[idx] + log1p(exp(-a[idx]))
    out[!idx] <- log1p(exp(a[!idx]))
    out
  }

  obj <- function(theta) {
    eta <- drop(Z %*% theta)
    mean(log1pexp(eta)) - sum(theta * b)
  }

  if (is.null(start)) {
    dat <- data.frame(y = yl, Xl)
    fit0 <- try(glm(y ~ ., family = binomial(), data = dat), silent = TRUE)

    if (inherits(fit0, "try-error")) {
      theta <- rep(0, p)
    } else {
      theta <- unname(coef(fit0))
      if (any(!is.finite(theta))) theta <- rep(0, p)
    }
  } else {
    theta <- as.numeric(start)
  }

  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    eta <- drop(Z %*% theta)
    pi <- plogis(eta)
    w <- pi * (1 - pi)

    grad <- drop(crossprod(Z, pi)) / n - b
    Hess <- crossprod(Z, Z * w) / n

    step <- solve(Hess, grad)

    # Backtracking line search for stability
    old.obj <- obj(theta)
    lambda <- 1

    repeat {
      theta.new <- theta - lambda * step
      new.obj <- obj(theta.new)

      if (new.obj <= old.obj || lambda < 1e-8) break
      lambda <- lambda / 2
    }

    if (trace) {
      cat("iter =", iter,
          " obj =", new.obj,
          " step =", max(abs(lambda * step)), "\n")
    }

    if (max(abs(lambda * step)) < tol * (1 + max(abs(theta)))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      break
    }

    theta <- theta.new
  }

  names(theta) <- c("beta0", paste0("beta", seq_len(ncol(Xl))))

  list(
    coef = theta,
    iterations = iter,
    gradient = grad,
    converged = iter < maxit
  )
}
```

---

## 5) Semi-supervised estimator and test performance

Using the above function:

```r
Xu <- xs[-(1:n1), ]

fit.tilde <- ssl_logit_newton(
  Xl = Xl,
  yl = yl,
  Xu = Xu,
  start = theta.hat
)

theta.tilde <- fit.tilde$coef

theta.tilde
perf(theta.tilde, xstest, ystest)
```

A compact table comparing the labeled MLE and semi-supervised estimator is:

```r
out <- rbind(
  labeled_MLE = c(theta.hat, perf(theta.hat, xstest, ystest)),
  semi_supervised = c(theta.tilde, perf(theta.tilde, xstest, ystest))
)

round(out, 4)
```

This reports \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\), its average test log-likelihood, and its test classification accuracy.

---

## 6) Plot training data with three classification lines

The logistic classification line for coefficient vector \(\theta=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)\) is

\[
\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2=0.
\]

If \(\beta_2\neq 0\), this is

\[
x_2=-\frac{\beta_0}{\beta_2}-\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}x_1.
\]

The third line is from the ordinary logistic MLE using all training labels `ys`.

```r
dat.all <- data.frame(
  y = ys,
  x1 = xs[, 1],
  x2 = xs[, 2]
)

fit.all <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial(), data = dat.all)

theta.all <- unname(coef(fit.all))
names(theta.all) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

draw_line <- function(theta, col, lty, lwd = 2) {
  if (abs(theta[3]) > 1e-12) {
    abline(
      a = -theta[1] / theta[3],
      b = -theta[2] / theta[3],
      col = col,
      lty = lty,
      lwd = lwd
    )
  } else {
    abline(
      v = -theta[1] / theta[2],
      col = col,
      lty = lty,
      lwd = lwd
    )
  }
}

plot(
  xs[, 1], xs[, 2],
  col = "grey80",
  pch = 1,
  xlab = expression(X[1]),
  ylab = expression(X[2]),
  main = "Labeled and unlabeled training data with classification lines"
)

points(
  xs[1:n1, 1], xs[1:n1, 2],
  col = ifelse(ys[1:n1] == 1, "tomato", "steelblue"),
  pch = 19
)

draw_line(theta.hat, col = "black", lty = 1)
draw_line(theta.tilde, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)
draw_line(theta.all, col = "purple", lty = 3)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c(
    "unlabeled",
    "labeled Y=0",
    "labeled Y=1",
    "labeled MLE",
    "semi-supervised",
    "all-label MLE"
  ),
  col = c("grey80", "steelblue", "tomato", "black", "darkgreen", "purple"),
  pch = c(1, 19, 19, NA, NA, NA),
  lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 1, 2, 3),
  lwd = c(NA, NA, NA, 2, 2, 2),
  bty = "n"
)
```

This produces the requested plot with the labeled-data MLE line, the semi-supervised line, and the all-label MLE line.

    grad <- drop(crossprod(Z, pi)) / n - b
    Hess <- crossprod(Z, Z * w) / n

    step <- solve(Hess, grad)

    # Backtracking line search for stability
    old.obj <- obj(theta)
    lambda <- 1

    repeat {
      theta.new <- theta - lambda * step
      new.obj <- obj(theta.new)

      if (new.obj <= old.obj || lambda < 1e-8) break
      lambda <- lambda / 2
    }

    if (trace) {
      cat("iter =", iter,
          " obj =", new.obj,
          " step =", max(abs(lambda * step)), "\n")
    }

    if (max(abs(lambda * step)) < tol * (1 + max(abs(theta)))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      break
    }

    theta <- theta.new
  }

  names(theta) <- c("beta0", paste0("beta", seq_len(ncol(Xl))))

  list(
    coef = theta,
    iterations = iter,
    gradient = grad,
    converged = iter < maxit
  )
}
```

## 5) Semi-supervised estimator and test performance

Using the above function:

```r
Xu <- xs[-(1:n1), ]

fit.tilde <- ssl_logit_newton(
  Xl = Xl,
  yl = yl,
  Xu = Xu,
  start = theta.hat
)

theta.tilde <- fit.tilde$coef

theta.tilde
perf(theta.tilde, xstest, ystest)
```

A compact table comparing the labeled MLE and semi-supervised estimator is:

```r
out <- rbind(
  labeled_MLE = c(theta.hat, perf(theta.hat, xstest, ystest)),
  semi_supervised = c(theta.tilde, perf(theta.tilde, xstest, ystest))
)

round(out, 4)
```

This reports \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\), its average test log-likelihood, and its test classification accuracy.

## 6) Plot training data with three classification lines

The logistic classification line for coefficient vector \(\theta=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)\) is

\[
\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2=0.
\]

If \(\beta_2\neq 0\), this is

\[
x_2=-\frac{\beta_0}{\beta_2}-\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}x_1.
\]

The third line is from the ordinary logistic MLE using all training labels `ys`.

```r
dat.all <- data.frame(
  y = ys,
  x1 = xs[, 1],
  x2 = xs[, 2]
)

fit.all <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial(), data = dat.all)

theta.all <- unname(coef(fit.all))
names(theta.all) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

draw_line <- function(theta, col, lty, lwd = 2) {
  if (abs(theta[3]) > 1e-12) {
    abline(
      a = -theta[1] / theta[3],
      b = -theta[2] / theta[3],
      col = col,
      lty = lty,
      lwd = lwd
    )
  } else {
    abline(
      v = -theta[1] / theta[2],
      col = col,
      lty = lty,
      lwd = lwd
    )
  }
}

plot(
  xs[, 1], xs[, 2],
  col = "grey80",
  pch = 1,
  xlab = expression(X[1]),
  ylab = expression(X[2]),
  main = "Labeled and unlabeled training data with classification lines"
)

points(
  xs[1:n1, 1], xs[1:n1, 2],
  col = ifelse(ys[1:n1] == 1, "tomato", "steelblue"),
  pch = 19
)

draw_line(theta.hat, col = "black", lty = 1)
draw_line(theta.tilde, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)
draw_line(theta.all, col = "purple", lty = 3)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c(
    "unlabeled",
    "labeled Y=0",
    "labeled Y=1",
    "labeled MLE",
    "semi-supervised",
    "all-label MLE"
  ),
  col = c("grey80", "steelblue", "tomato", "black", "darkgreen", "purple"),
  pch = c(1, 19, 19, NA, NA, NA),
  lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 1, 2, 3),
  lwd = c(NA, NA, NA, 2, 2, 2),
  bty = "n"
)
```

This produces the requested plot with the labeled-data MLE line, the semi-supervised line, and the all-label MLE line.
